construction: 12 parts in 2 steps. Step 1: the engine core, a 43121 shell with the 46667 fan pushed into its front, four bushes on the fan pin, and at the back a 2×2 round plate, a four-prong spider (LDraw part 2566, catalogued as an obsolete palm-tree top) and the 3942c cone pointing aft as the exhaust. Step 2: the pylon, a 2×8 plate laid along the engine with a 6×2 curved slope and an inverted 3×2 slope on top closing the fairing.
interfaces: Stud directions: 12 parts, 10 up, 2 facing +Z (the round plate and cone on the exhaust axis). The pylon plate's studs are the only mounting interface; it meets the anti-studs under the 54093 wing. The fan turns on its pin; nothing else moves.
lesson: A convincing jet nacelle from three dedicated parts (43121 engine shell, 46667 fan on its own pin, 3942c cone as the exhaust) hung under the wing on a thin pylon: a 2×8 plate with a 6×2 curved slope and an inverted 33° slope as its fairing.
parent_context: `7893 - plane.ldr` places it four times with the identity matrix at X ±220 (Z −80) and X ±380 (Z 0), all at Y 32: two engines per wing, the outboard pair one stud further aft. The wing underside supplies the anti-studs; the engines hang below the wing plane.
reuse_notes: Use it for any twin- or four-engine airliner: keep the fan, shell and cone on one axis, mount through the pylon plate only, and space repeated engines along the wing sweep. Swap the pylon fairing slopes to change the pylon profile.
